rules.section_title: Préambule > 1 Abbreviations, acronyms and signs
rules.rule_text: Abbreviations and acronyms are commonly used in both formal and informal writing to increase readability and conciseness. However, improper use can lead to confusion and misinterpretation.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 1 Abbreviations, acronyms and signs > General rules
rules.rule_text:
· An abbreviation is a shortened form of a word or phrase (Prof for Professor or etc. for et cetera).

· An acronym is a word formed from the initial letters of a phrase (OECD, EU). Acronyms can be pronounced letter by letter (OECD) or as a word (NATO).

· Lists of common abbreviations are provided below.

See also: Bibliographical references, citations and notes; Country and territory names, codes and currencies, and territorial disclaimers; Dates and time; Numbers and units of measure; The OECD and other international organisations; Translation and terms in other languages.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 1 Abbreviations, acronyms and signs > General rules > Do
rules.rule_text:
:selected: Always spell out the full form of a term on the first use in a document followed by the abbreviation or acronym in parentheses. Once introduced, use the abbreviation or acronym consistently throughout the text.

Always double check that the acronym is correct, referring to that used by source institution or entity.

/ Use abbreviations and acronyms that are well known to your audience. If you have many, or if you must use lesser-known ones for technical terms, provide a list of definitions.

Only use abbreviations or acronyms in figures, infographics and tables if space constraints are significant. Ensure that those used are explained in the surrounding text on first usage.

/ Use uppercase letters without full stops for acronyms, whether they are pronounced as a word (NATO) or read letter by letter (OECD).

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) launched the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) in 1997. More than 80 countries participated in PISA in 2023.

/ For acronyms originating from another language, use the widely accepted English name in full and include original name and acronym in parentheses. If the term is used frequently in the text, consider adding a list of all acronyms and abbreviations and use the original acronym in the text. The National Digital Strategy Office (Coordinación de la Estrategia Digital Nacional, CEDN)

/ Use the " symbol when noting the copyright of an image or photo (@ Author name/Image bank name): @ J. Smith/Shutterstock.com.

/ Use "the" before an acronym only if it is read letter by letter ("the UN" but "UNESCO" or "ESA" not "the ESA").

rules.section_title: Préambule > 1 Abbreviations, acronyms and signs > General rules > Don't
rules.rule_text:
Don't: X Overuse acronyms and abbreviations; only introduce them if a term occurs frequently. :selected:

x Invent abbreviations or use non-standard ones. :selected:

x Use full stops (periods) in common abbreviations and acronyms unless they are part of a formal :selected: name or established convention.

x Use an apostrophe when pluralising acronyms. :selected:

X Use "the" before the acronym if it being used as an adjective (OECD experts agreed ... ). :selected: There are many IO's in the UN system (W.H.O.).

@ There are many IOs in the UN system (the WHO).

x Abbreviate months or days of the week in full text, titles or subtitles; only abbreviate in figures, :selected: infographics or tables if space is limited.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 2 Bibliographical references, citations and notes
rules.rule_text: Bibliographical references and citations provide the necessary information for readers to locate and verify the sources used in the document. Proper acknowledgement of source materials ensures the credibility, transparency and accessibility of OECD content.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 2 Bibliographical references, citations and notes > General rules
rules.rule_text:
· All OECD authors are required to provide the sources for concepts, data and quotations used in their publications.

· The OECD provides a citation tool, Mendeley, available through O.N.E Author.

· Citing your sources as you draft saves time.

See also: Capitalisation; Italics, roman and bold type; Punctuation.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 2 Bibliographical references, citations and notes > Citing sources in-text
rules.rule_text:
· All source material, whether printed or digital, whether a publication or a media or multimedia product, can be cited in-text, following the rules below.

· By providing key information in parentheses, in-text citations provide immediate reference to sources without interrupting the flow of reading.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 2 Bibliographical references, citations and notes > Citing sources in-text > Do
rules.rule_text:
/ Use the author-date system for in-text citations. :selected: o For one author, include the author's surname and the year of publication, as well as page :unselected: number(s) if desired.

o For up to three authors, list all; for four or more authors, use the first author's surname and :unselected: "et al.".

o When several works are cited in the same place, cite them within parentheses, separated by :unselected: semi-colons.

o The author(s) may also be cited by name followed by the publication date in parentheses. :unselected:

o For forthcoming works, list the author's surname and "forthcoming". :unselected:

o For unpublished works, list the author's surname and "unpublished". :unselected:

o For works without a publication date, list the author's surname and "n.d.".

/ See the table "In-text citations" for examples. :selected:

Ensure that for each source you cite in-text, the full citation appears in your reference list. :selected:

rules.section_title: Préambule > 2 Bibliographical references, citations and notes > Citing sources in-text > Don't
rules.rule_text:
Don't: X Include excessive in-text citations in a single sentence, integrate them meaningfully. :selected:

x Make generic statements without proper sourcing. :selected:

x Place source citations in footnotes or endnotes. :selected:

rules.section_title: Préambule > 2 Bibliographical references, citations and notes > Referencing legal documents and legislation
rules.rule_text:
· Legal references should generally include the key relevant information, such as the issuing body, document title, and date, as well as URL if available and date accessed if appropriate.

· When citing legal documentation, domestic citation standards should be followed (e.g. the case law of the French Conseil d'Etat should be cited in the same way that the Conseil d'État cites its own jurisprudence).

· Many OECD Member countries maintain style guides for their national printing offices as well as databases of legislation, which may be consulted online.

· When citing legal documentation of other international organisations, the standards developed by those organisations should be followed (e.g. Directives of the European Parliament and of the Council should be cited according to EU practice).

· When referencing OECD legal instruments adopted by the OECD Council or within the framework of the OECD, the style will differ depending on whether the legal instrument is mentioned in the body of a text or included in the bibliography. Follow the examples in "Referencing OECD legal instruments".

rules.section_title: Préambule > 3 Capitalisation
rules.rule_text: Using capitalisation correctly is important for clarity and consistency, while excessive capitalisation distracts from readability. Correct usage allows the reader to distinguish between proper nouns and other words and to identify visually different content types as well as levels of hierarchy in text.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 3 Capitalisation > General rules
rules.rule_text:
· Capitalise the first letter of a word that begins a sentence and all proper nouns (names of events, persons, places, organisations, nationalities and languages).

· For titles and subtitles of books, periodicals and series, use title case.

· For all other titles and subtitles, use sentence case. If a title includes a colon, capitalise the first word following the colon.

. In most cases, specific terms may be capitalised; general terms should never be capitalised.

See also: Abbreviations, acronyms and signs; Country and territory names, codes and currencies, and territorial disclaimers.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 3 Capitalisation > OECD Members and Partners
rules.rule_text:
· Capitalise Member in "OECD Member", "OECD Members", "OECD Member country" and "OECD Member countries", as well as in "non-Member".

· Capitalise both words in Key Partners (Brazil, China, India, Indonesia and South Africa).

· Do not capitalise accession or accession candidate country.

· Capitalise Associate, Participant and Invitee if the terms are being used in the context of non-Member participation in the work of in OECD subsidiary bodies in line with the general principals set out in Revised Resolution of the Council on Partnerships in OECD Bodies [C(2012)100/REV2/FINAL].

· Do not capitalise these terms when they are used as common nouns.

· Do not capitalise the term observer.

See also: The OECD and other international organisations.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 3 Capitalisation > Publications
rules.rule_text:
· Publication titles and subtitles use either title case or sentence case, depending on the content type (reports, papers, policy briefs, country notes and case studies).

· In title case, each word is capitalised except for conjunctions or adverbs.

· In sentence case, only the first word is capitalised, except for any proper nouns included.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 3 Capitalisation > Publications > Do
rules.rule_text:
:selected: / Use title case for report titles and subtitles, the names of projects or initiatives, and country notes when referring to the name of the "parent" publication.

o If a title includes a colon, capitalise the first word following it. :unselected:

o If a title includes a hyphenated adjectival phrase, capitalise both parts. :unselected: The OECD has released a new report, Evidence-Based Decision Making in Health Policy.

/ Use sentence case for the titles and subtitles of report chapters, papers and short content.

For all other titles and subtitles (including those of boxes, figures, infographics and tables) use sentence case.

/ Use sentence case references to specific components of a report (e.g. chapters, annexes, boxes, figures, infographics and tables).

rules.section_title: Préambule > 4 Country and territory names, codes and currencies, and territorial disclaimers
rules.rule_text: Referring to countries and territories incorrectly or depicting them in maps inaccurately can raise diplomatic sensitivities. To avoid this, follow the guidance provided by the Directorate for Legal Affairs and the Directorate for Communications regarding country and territory names and codes, currency codes and symbols, territorial disclaimers, and maps.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 4 Country and territory names, codes and currencies, and territorial disclaimers > Country and territory names
rules.rule_text:
· The OECD has specific naming and style conventions for Members, non-Members, Key Partners and accession candidate countries.

· The Directorate for Legal Affairs (LEG) provides a list of the official country and territory long names, short names, names in lists, tables, maps and graphics, and ISO codes, to be used in OECD content:

https://portal.oecd.org/eshare/leg/Pages/Home.aspx#Countries%2c%20Territories%20and%20Di plomatic%20Sensitivities.

. If in doubt, or if asked to apply different naming, contact LEGILU@oecd.org for clarification.

. Use these names in all content, regardless of format and of whether it is published externally or remains internal.

· Remember that there are small differences in spelling between many names in English and French; always check the spelling is correct for the language in which you are drafting and refer to the table at the end of this chapter.

See also: Abbreviations, acronyms and signs; The OECD and other international organisations.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 4 Country and territory names, codes and currencies, and territorial disclaimers > Country and territory names > Do
rules.rule_text:
Only use the country and territory names and codes included in the list provided by LEG.

Use the long name the first time a country or territory is mentioned in the text of the document, define the short name for what follows, then use the short name thereafter.

The Republic of Türkiye (hereafter "Türkiye") is a Member of the OECD. Türkiye was one of the 20 founders of the OECD in 1960.

/ Add "the" before these countries: the Netherlands, the Russian Federation, the Slovak Republic, the United Kingdom and the United States. These countries always take the singular verb form.

/ Use "Euro area" when referring to the 20 EU Member States that use the euro.

Spell out country and territory names in full when used as nouns (the United States, the United Kingdom) but use abbreviations when used as adjectives (US companies, UAE delegates, UK unions).

/ Always list countries and territories alphabetically (in English) in text unless LEG's list advises otherwise. Take care to check in LEG's list for any exceptions; for example, the People's Republic of China is listed under "C" (China, the People's Republic of). If no letter is specified, the entry is under the first letter of the country or territory's name ("R" for the Russian Federation).

/ Countries and territories may be listed non-alphabetically if there is a specific reason for another order, such as a ranking.

The top three performing countries were Japan, Canada and New Zealand.

rules.rule_text: · Given the sensitive nature of any visual representation of a country or territory, such as a map, a flag, an emoji, an image, or a photo, use such representations only with moderation and caution.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 4 Country and territory names, codes and currencies, and territorial disclaimers > Visual representations of countries and territories > Do

rules.rule_text:
· ISO codes for countries and territories should generally be avoided, as the ISO country and territory names to which they relate do not align with OECD practice. In cases where the use of ISO codes is necessary, a table setting out the ISO codes and the country or territory names to which they relate (in line with LEG guidance) should be added in a reader's guide.

· Consult LEG's "List of names of countries and territories and related guidelines" available at https://portal.oecd.org/eshare/leg/Pages/Home.aspx.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 4 Country and territory names, codes and currencies, and territorial disclaimers > ISO currency codes
rules.rule_text:
· Currencies can be designated by terms, codes or symbols.

· To avoid confusion, use the ISO code for specific currencies and the term for generic references. The budget is USD 5 million but the budget is millions of dollars.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 4 Country and territory names, codes and currencies, and territorial disclaimers > ISO currency codes > Do
rules.rule_text:
Use the currency code in publications, short content and web copy. Use the currency symbol if necessary due to space constraints in social media or in figures and tables.

/ Place the code before the amount (USD 1 000), separated by a hard space; place symbol before the amount without a space ($1 000). Place the term after the amount (1 000 dollars), separated by a hard space.

Define uncommon currency codes on first use in the text. In order to finance the merger, the company raised KGS 5 million (Kyrgyz Republic soms).

V For uncommon currencies, indicate the equivalent in a more common currency (EUR, USD). The bank allocated IQD 1 billion (USD 750 millions) to the project.

/ For web and social media content, currency symbols can be used, but replace with currency codes :selected: if there is a risk of confusion.

Australia contributed $100 million in aid, the United States contributed $100 million.

@ Australia contributed AUD 100 million in aid, the United States contributed USD 100 million.

Refer to the tables below for the currency names, codes and symbols for OECD Members and the :selected: euro area.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 5 Dates and time
rules.rule_text: With membership and engagement around the world, it is important to refer to dates, time and seasons in a simple and consistent way, in order to prevent ambiguity and inaccuracy.

y For dates in technical documents and datasets, use the format DD-MM-YYYY. :selected:

See also: Abbreviations for days; Abbreviations for months.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 6 Hyphenation
rules.rule_text: Used correctly, hyphens improve the clarity of your text and help you to avoid ambiguity. They are essential for compound words and terms.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 6 Hyphenation > General rules
rules.rule_text:
· A hyphen joins words or parts of words to form a compound adjective, adverb, noun or verb.

· Hyphens provide clarity. For example, "A small business owner" and "A small-business owner": the first is a small owner of a business; the second is owns a small business.

· Non-breaking hyphens should be used all instances throughout Word™ text in which the words should be displayed on the same line in the final output

· When in doubt, consult the word's entry in the Oxford English Dictionary.

See also: Capitalisation.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 6 Hyphenation > Policy maker, policy-maker or policymaker? Frequent hyphenation questions
rules.rule_text:
· Use policymaker (noun) and policymaking (noun and adjective); do not hyphenate.

· Use decision maker (noun) and decision making (noun and adjective); do not hyphenate.

· Use macroeconomics (noun), macroeconomic (adjective), microeconomics (noun) and microeconomic (adjective); do not hyphenate.

· Hyphenate socio-economics (noun) and socio-economic (adjective).

· Use online as both an adjective and adverb; do not hyphenate or split into two words.

· Use website as one word without hyphenation but use web page and web manager as two-word phrases, without hyphenation.

· Use worldwide as both an adjective and adverb; do not hyphenate or split into two words.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 6 Hyphenation > Adjectives and adverbs
rules.rule_text: · When two words together act as a compound adjective modifying a noun, they are generally hyphenated.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 6 Hyphenation > Adjectives and adverbs > Do
rules.rule_text:
y Use hyphens in compound adjectives before nouns ("attributive" adjectives). The report takes an evidence-based approach.

The well-known economist addressed the conference.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 6 Hyphenation > Adjectives and adverbs > Don't
rules.rule_text:
Don't: x Hyphenate compound adjectives when the first word is an adverb ending in "-ly". :selected: Targeted training programmes should help to develop a highly-skilled workforce.

@ Targeted training programmes should help to develop a highly skilled workforce.

x Use a hyphen if the compound adjective comes after a preposition or noun ("predicate" adjectives). :selected: In the longer-term, the policy measures will boost employment.

In the longer term, the policy measures will boost employment.

The recommendations are evidence-based.

The recommendations are evidence based.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 6 Hyphenation > Adjectives and adverbs > Do
rules.rule_text:
Capitalise proper nouns in compound words; if a hyphenated term contains a proper noun and a common element, only capitalise the proper noun.

The group was founded to promote Anglo-American relations. Quebec is a French-speaking region in Canada.

For title case, capitalise the second word in a hyphenated term.

The OECD has released a new report, Evidence-Based Decision Making in Health Policy.

For joint works, separate the abbreviations or acronyms of the two organisations with a hyphen. The OECD-FAO Agricultural Outlook.

See also: Capitalisation; Country and territory names, codes and currencies, and territorial disclaimers.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 6 Hyphenation > Adjectives and adverbs > Don't
rules.rule_text:
Don't: X Capitalise common elements unless they begin the title, heading or sentence. :selected: The problem cannot be solved with Short-term solutions.

Short-term solutions cannot solve the problem.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 6 Hyphenation > Dangling hyphens
rules.rule_text:
· Hyphens are often used to show that two or more compound terms share a common part.

· Use them sparingly where the sense is clear and be consistent in your use throughout your text.

See also: Punctuation.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 6 Hyphenation > Dangling hyphens > Do
rules.rule_text: Repeat the hyphenated prefix for clarity. :selected: The article compared pre- and post-pandemic data.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 6 Hyphenation > Dangling hyphens > Don't
rules.rule_text:
Don't: x Use dangling hyphens if omitting the term creates confusion. :selected: The university offers courses for under- and postgraduate students.

The university offers courses for undergraduate and postgraduate students.

X Omit the second hyphen, or subsequent hyphens, as this may create confusion. :selected: The course is required for first-, second and third year students.

The course is required for first-, second- and third-year students.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 6 Hyphenation > Doubled hyphens
rules.rule_text: · Compounds made of more than two words may use multiple hyphens. The working party met to discuss balance-of-payment deficits.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 6 Hyphenation > Doubled hyphens > Do
rules.rule_text:
V Be consistent in your use of double hyphens throughout your text. :selected:

Hyphenate the number range in ages: :selected: o If the age range is being used as an adjective, hyphenate all parts of the compound phrase. :unselected:

The survey assessed the annual earnings of 15-to-24-year-old workers.

o If the age range is being used as a noun, do not include "to" and drop hyphen after the last :unselected: figure.

The study examines the number of 15-19 year-olds who leave school without a qualification.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 6 Hyphenation > Doubled hyphens > Don't
rules.rule_text: Don't: x Overuse doubled hyphens; rephrase as needed. :selected: A non-self-financing institution. The institution is financed by donors.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 6 Hyphenation > Non-breaking hyphens
rules.rule_text:
· Use non-breaking hyphens when you want to keep a word or number on the same line, in order to preserve meaning and enhancing readability.

· Be aware that non-breaking hyphens must be used all instances throughout Word™ text where the words should be displayed on the same line in the final output.

· Insert a non-breaking hyphen using (Ctrl + 8).

rules.section_title: Préambule > 6 Hyphenation > Non-breaking hyphens > Do
rules.rule_text:
/ Use non-breaking hyphens for terms proper nouns, numbers, negative sums, years, abbreviations :selected: and acronyms.

See also: Negative numbers.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 6 Hyphenation > Non-breaking hyphens > Don't
rules.rule_text:
Don't: X Allow line breaks to separate critical compound terms. :selected:

x Use non-breaking hyphens to systematically replace all hyphens. :selected:

rules.section_title: Préambule > 6 Hyphenation > Prefixes
rules.rule_text:
· Hyphenation with prefixes depends on established usage and clarity.

· Compounds formed with prefixes are often standard combined words rather than hyphenated, whether they are adjectives, adverbs, nouns or verbs (upfront, underdeveloped, overestimate).

· Adding a prefix to create a compound word often requires a hyphen (ex. cross-country, intra- industry, non-tradeable).

rules.section_title: Préambule > 6 Hyphenation > Prefixes > Do
rules.rule_text:
:selected: / Use hyphens after prefixes for clarity, following established usage. Consult the Oxford English Dictionary if in doubt.

The report provides a cross-country analysis of education systems.

/ Hyphenate to prevent confusion with other words. :selected:

He was asked to re-sign [sign again] the form vs. He resigned from [left] the group.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 6 Hyphenation > Prefixes > Don't
rules.rule_text:
Don't: x Hyphenate when the prefix and root are commonly combined. :selected: The team will re-write the proposal.

The team will rewrite the proposal.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 6 Hyphenation > Prefixes > Do
rules.rule_text:
:selected: / Hyphenate double vowels and double or triple consonants (co-ordinate, re-entry, non-negotiable, shell-like).

:selected: / Hyphenate when a prefix and root word result in double letters and the meaning may be ambiguous.

She bought her chicken coop [cage or pen] at the gardening co-op [abbreviated term for a co-operative group or business].

rules.section_title: Préambule > 6 Hyphenation > Prefixes > Don't
rules.rule_text: Don't: x Omit the hyphen in our Organisation's name. :selected: Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development

rules.section_title: Préambule > 7 Inclusive language
rules.rule_text: Using inclusive language reflects the OECD's commitment to equality, diversity and inclusion, ensuring that content is respectful, accurate and accessible to a global audience.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 7 Inclusive language > General advice
rules.rule_text:
· Use neutral, factual language and exclude outdated or offensive terms.

· Be respectful - use the terms that individuals and communities use to refer to themselves. When in doubt, ask relevant stakeholders and COM.

· Be aware that language evolves and there is always more to learn.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 7 Inclusive language > Age
rules.rule_text: · Certain terms used to describe older adults may reinforce negative stereotypes about the health and competence of individuals older than 60.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 7 Inclusive language > Age > Do
rules.rule_text:
/ Prefer "older" to "elderly" and avoid terms such as "seniors". Older people are living longer, healthier lives than ever before.

/ Use balanced age comparisons: "younger, middle-aged and older adults". The survey includes samples from younger and older populations.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 7 Inclusive language > Disability
rules.rule_text:
· Whether and how to address ability and disability depends on whether it is contextually necessary and on the terminology preferences of the individuals and communities involved.

· People-first language emphasises the individual rather than their disability or condition (a person with a traumatic brain injury) and their lived experience.

· Identity-first language puts focus on the disability, as a way of reclaiming identity (a Deaf person).

rules.section_title: Préambule > 7 Inclusive language > Disability > Do
rules.rule_text:
/ Use people-first language in most cases.

/ Use identity-first language if requested by an individual or community.

@ The workspace now has ramps to accommodate handicapped people.

@ The workspace design facilitates mobility for people who use wheelchairs.

Avoid negative framing such as "suffers from" or "victim of".

The centre provides activities for Down Syndrome children and other children suffering from congenital disabilities.

@ The centre provides activities for children living with Down Syndrome and other congenital disabilities.

rules.rule_text:
:selected:

· Gender-neutral language removes assumptions about gender identity, gender roles and relationships.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 7 Inclusive language > Gender-neutral language > Do
rules.rule_text:

/ Use the phrase "different genders" rather than "opposite genders". :selected:

rules.section_title: Préambule > 7 Inclusive language > Personal pronouns
rules.rule_text: . Many people use the standard English pronouns "she/her" and "he/his"; others use "they/them" or other forms.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 7 Inclusive language > Personal pronouns > Do
rules.rule_text:
v Avoid gender pronouns unless needed for specific context; often a sentence is just as clear without the pronoun.

Each candidate will be asked to finish his test within 30 minutes.

@ Each candidate will be asked to finish the test within 30 minutes.

V Refer to individuals by their self-identified pronouns, whether speaking or writing.

/ Use gender-neutral pronouns ("they/them") as singular pronouns when gender is unknown, rather than male or female pronouns, or rephrase to avoid using a pronoun.

Someone left her backpack in the conference room.

Someone left their backpack in the conference room.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 7 Inclusive language > Race and ethnicity
rules.rule_text:
. It is imperative to avoid terms that are outdated, offensive, perpetuate stereotypes or imply value judgments.

· Whenever possible, use the racial and/or ethnic terms that the individuals or communities being discussed use themselves.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 7 Inclusive language > Race and ethnicity > Do
rules.rule_text:
Reference cultural or ethnic identifiers only when relevant to the content.

Use terms preferred by the individual or groups described. When in doubt, ask.

/ Prefer specific terms to generic terms.

The roundtable was made up of Asian policymakers.

@ The roundtable was made up of policymakers from Japan, Korea and Thailand.

/ Use "minority" as an adjective rather than a noun when referring to individuals and groups.

@ The report analyses educational outcomes of minorities in five countries.

The report analyses the educational outcomes of minority groups in five countries.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 7 Inclusive language > Sexual orientation
rules.rule_text:
. The language used to describe sexual orientation should be inclusive, respectful and free from assumptions or bias.

· Whenever possible, use accurate and affirming terms that the individuals or communities being discussed use themselves.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 7 Inclusive language > Sexual orientation > Do
rules.rule_text:
/ Use accurate and affirming terms to refer to LGBTIQ+ communities. :selected: The survey asked participants to indicate their sexual preference. @ The survey asked participants to describe their sexual orientation.

Avoid terms that imply a preference or are medically outdated. :selected:

Only reference sexual orientation where relevant or pertinent. :selected:

/ Avoid language that explicitly assumes gender identity. :selected: New households are formed following the marriage of a man and a woman.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 8 Italics, roman and bold type
rules.rule_text: Different kinds and weight of typeface help readers to understand the function of a word or phrase or their importance.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 8 Italics, roman and bold type > General rules
rules.rule_text: · Use the styles in O.N.E Author to organise your information and to format your titles and headings. Do not apply bold, italics or underlining to create a hierarchy of information.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 8 Italics, roman and bold type > Italic type
rules.rule_text:
. Reserve its use for specific elements that need emphasis or differentiation.

· Use sparingly to ensure readability on screen and in print and to preserve its utility for emphasis.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 8 Italics, roman and bold type > Italic type > Do
rules.rule_text:
:selected: / Italicise titles of reports, books, journals, newspapers, magazines, databases, and working and policy paper series names. Do not put quotation marks around italicised titles (OECD Employment Outlook 2025; Moby Dick; The Economist).

/ Italicise words or phrases from other languages that are not yet naturalised in English. :selected: The nation's policy of autarky stifled international trade opportunities.

/ Use italics for technical terms or variables upon first mention. :selected: The variable X represents economic output.

/ Write Latin abbreviations in italics, except for those listed in the table "Latin terms and abbreviations :selected: to put in roman type".

rules.section_title: Préambule > 8 Italics, roman and bold type > Italic type > Don't
rules.rule_text:
Don't: :selected: x Overuse italics for emphasis. Excessive use sounds informal, hinders readability and reduces its value for emphasis.

x Italicise common words or terms from other languages that are widely understood in English (per capita, laissez-faire, modus operandi). :selected:

x Italicise titles of sections, chapters, or articles within a publication, or paper titles. Use roman type with double quotation marks instead. :selected:

X Italicise URLs. :selected:

rules.section_title: Préambule > 8 Italics, roman and bold type > Roman type
rules.rule_text: . Roman type is the default style for the body text and is used for most elements in OECD publications.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 8 Italics, roman and bold type > Roman type > Do
rules.rule_text:
/ Use roman type for titles of sections, chapters, articles, papers, policy briefs, country notes, case :selected: studies and documents, enclosing them in double quotation marks. Chapter 4 is titled "Sustainable growth strategies in Europe".

:selected: / Use roman type for the titles of programmes, legislation, codes and declarations, names of organisations, and proper nouns; do not use italics or bold. Capitalise as appropriate. The OECD and the ADB collaborated on the project. The Paris Agreement was adopted by 196 parties.

/ Default to roman type for foreign terms that are commonly used in English. :selected: The results are calculated per capita.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 8 Italics, roman and bold type > Roman type > Don't
rules.rule_text:
Don't: x Use roman type for titles of reports, books and periodicals. :selected:

x Use roman type for words or phrases from other languages that are not yet naturalised in English. :selected:

rules.section_title: Préambule > 8 Italics, roman and bold type > Using italic and roman type together
rules.rule_text: · Pay attention to how you mix italic and roman type together, to ensure clarity and consistency.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 8 Italics, roman and bold type > Using italic and roman type together > Do
rules.rule_text:
Note that when the body of a text is in italics, items that normally would be italicised become roman.

:selected: Literacy and numeracy skills among adults have largely declined or stagnated over the past decade, according to the second OECD Survey of Adult Skills, published this week.

:selected: / Switch back to roman type for punctuation immediately following italicised words unless the punctuation is part of the italicised phrase.

The report How's Life in the Digital Age? has assembled 33 indicators of key impacts of the digital transformation.

Have you read the latest edition of the OECD Pensions Outlook?

rules.section_title: Préambule > 8 Italics, roman and bold type > Bold
rules.rule_text: · Bold is reserved for signalling emphasis.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 8 Italics, roman and bold type > Bold > Do
rules.rule_text: / Use very sparingly, only if essential for meaning. Bold can be considered aggressive looking if :selected: overused.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 8 Italics, roman and bold type > Bold > Don't
rules.rule_text: Don't: x Apply bold as a formatting choice to indicate hierarchy. Use the style settings available in :selected: O.N.E Author instead.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 8 Italics, roman and bold type > Underlining
rules.rule_text:
· Underlining gives an informal and unprofessional look to your text.

· It can also be mistaken for a hyperlink.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 8 Italics, roman and bold type > Underlining > Don't
rules.rule_text: Don't: x Use underlining, unless it appears automatically as part of a URL. :selected:

rules.section_title: Préambule > 9 Numbers and units of measure
rules.rule_text: Correctly and consistently expressing numbers and units ensures the accuracy and reliability of OECD work. Be aware of differences between English and French common practices for numbers and units.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 9 Numbers and units of measure > General rules
rules.rule_text:
· Depending on the context, ordinal numbers can be written in words (one, two, three ... ), Arabic numerals (1, 2, 3 ... ), or Roman numerals (I, II, III ... ).

· There are small but significant differences in how numbers are expressed in English and French, explained in the table at the end of this chapter.

See also: Abbreviations, acronyms and signs; Dates and time; Hyphenation; Punctuation.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 9 Numbers and units of measure > Cardinal numbers
rules.rule_text: · Cardinal numbers express quantity and are used for counting. :selected:

rules.section_title: Préambule > 9 Numbers and units of measure > Cardinal numbers > Do
rules.rule_text:
/ Express one to ten in words, not figures, except for: :selected:

o numbers used with an ISO currency code (USD 6) :unselected:

o percentages (5%) :unselected:

o numbers associated with measurement units (3 km, 80 tonnes, 1 L) :unselected:

o when numbers less than ten and greater than ten occur together in context, write them all in :unselected: figures

At the meeting, 12 Member countries and 3 non-Member economies raised the issue.

o numbers followed by "million", "billion" or "trillion" (1 million, 3 billion, 5 trillion) :unselected:

o representing scale (on a scale of 0-10). :unselected:

/ Express numbers 11 and above in figures, not words.

/ When two numbers refer to one item, spell out one of them and express the other in figures, following the rules above.

They requested four 1-metre stands.

v Always write a number out in words if it is the first word in of a sentence.

Twelve OECD Member countries raised the same issue.

Always write a number out in words in titles or subtitles.

The report Learning beyond Fifteen: Ten Years of PISA was released in 2012.

V For web content, write numbers as digits, not words, with the thousands place separated by a hard space.

V For web content, write numbers as digits, not words.

Round off large numbers, particularly in text.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 9 Numbers and units of measure > 1.2 billion
rules.rule_text: See also: Breaks and hard spaces.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 9 Numbers and units of measure > 1.2 billion > Don't
rules.rule_text:
Don't: X Use roman numerals (I, II, III ... ), unless as part of an individual's title, the title of a work, or the title of an event or time period. :selected:

Mobile phones became widely used at the end of the XXth century.

Mobile phones became widely used at the end of the 20th century.

King Richard the 3rd of England died in 1485.

King Richard III of England died in 1485.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 9 Numbers and units of measure > 1.2 billion > Decimal fractions
rules.rule_text:
· Numbers containing decimal fractions should always be written in numbers.

· Decimal fractions are always plural.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 9 Numbers and units of measure > 1.2 billion > Decimal fractions > Do
rules.rule_text:
/ Express decimal fractions in numerals. :selected:

/ Use a decimal point, never a comma or other mark. :selected: The average family has 2.4 children.

v Use a zero, never a blank space. :selected:

rules.section_title: Préambule > 9 Numbers and units of measure > 0.45 (not .45)
rules.rule_text: Round currency up or down to a full number or give the number to two decimal places. :selected: AUS 1 (instead of AUS 0.92); USD 0.02 (for two cents) EUR 0.20 (for 20 cents).

rules.section_title: Préambule > 9 Numbers and units of measure > 0.45 (not .45) > Do
rules.rule_text:
/ Express non-decimal fractions in words. :selected:

/ Hyphenate the numbers in a fraction regardless of whether it is being used as an adjective or noun. :selected:

In general, use only readily recognisable fractions such as one-third, one-quarter, one-half. :selected: Three-quarters of the legislators voted for the resolution.

The Senate approved the bill by a two-thirds majority.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 9 Numbers and units of measure > 0.45 (not .45) > Don't
rules.rule_text:
Don't: X Use numerals to express non-decimal fractions. :selected: Over 1/4 of the class was absent.

Over one-fourth of the class was absent.

X Use less recognisable forms of fractions. :selected: The survey showed two-eighths of the territory was uninhabitable.

The survey showed that 25% of the territory was uninhabitable.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 9 Numbers and units of measure > 0.45 (not .45) > Negative numbers
rules.rule_text:
:selected:

· Negative numbers always have a value that is less than zero. This is indicated with a minus sign proceeding the numeral (-446.2).

rules.section_title: Préambule > 9 Numbers and units of measure > 0.45 (not .45) > Negative numbers > Do
rules.rule_text: y Use non-breaking space or the minus key for the minus sign, to ensure the sign and number stay :selected: on the same line.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 9 Numbers and units of measure > 0.45 (not .45) > Negative numbers > Don't
rules.rule_text:
Don't: x Leave a space between the minus sign and the number. :selected:

x If referring to currencies, put the ISO code first, then the negative number (CAD -225). :selected:

See also: Breaks and hard spaces; Hyphenation.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 9 Numbers and units of measure > 0.45 (not .45) > Ordinal numbers
rules.rule_text:
:selected:

· Ordinal numbers express position in an order or series.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 9 Numbers and units of measure > 0.45 (not .45) > Ordinal numbers > Do
rules.rule_text: / Use ordinal numbers sparingly. Overuse is distracting for the reader, particularly in lists. :selected:

rules.section_title: Préambule > 9 Numbers and units of measure > 0.45 (not .45) > Ordinal numbers > Don't
rules.rule_text:
Don't: :selected: x Use the adverbial form of ordinal numbers (firstly, secondly ... ). Reword the sentence.

@ The proposed legislation will help local businesses in two ways. Firstly, it will attract investment to the area. Secondly, it will fund training programmes.

The proposed legislation will help local businesses by attracting investment and funding training programmes.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 9 Numbers and units of measure > 0.45 (not .45) > Ordinal numbers > Do
rules.rule_text:
:selected: / Use "%" in all text and graphics, except in publication titles, chapter titles, section headings, and when the percentage is the first word of the sentence.

/ Use "%" or "per cent" in a text when referring to a defined amount. :selected:

/ Use "per cent" (not "%" or "percent") when the percentage expressed is the first word of the :selected:

sentence.

Ninety per cent of the participants agreed with the chair's proposal, but 10% did not.

/ Use "percentage" when referring to a general proportion or share. :selected: A small percentage of the students needed extra tutoring.

/ Spell out "percentage points" on first usage followed by (p.p.) and use "p.p." thereafter. :selected: The survival rate of supported firms was approximately 2.5 p.p. higher than the one of non- supported firms after 12 months.

:selected: In general, for a percentage that is a decimal fraction, round to one decimal point. If one or more percentages are a decimal fraction, express any whole number percentages in the same sentence or list with the whole number followed by ".0". The inflation rate was 2.2% in November 2024, up from 2.0% in October.

/ Repeat the % sign after each number in a series. :selected: Last week, 45%, 55% and 65% of the trains, planes and buses ran on time, respectively.

/ Repeat the "%" sign when per cent ranges are separated by prepositions but not when the range is hyphenated. :selected:

On average, 10% to 20% of food is wasted every day. On average, 10-20% of food is wasted every day.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 9 Numbers and units of measure > 0.45 (not .45) > Ordinal numbers > Don't
rules.rule_text:
Don't: x Use the "%" symbol with a number written as a word; use the numeral instead. :selected:

x Put a space between the number and the percentage sign. :selected: The hurricane damaged fifty % of the buildings.

The hurricane damaged 50% of the buildings.

x Use the % sign with non-decimal fractions. :selected: The price was cut by 1/4%.

The price was cut by 0.25%.

See also: Breaks and hard spaces.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 9 Numbers and units of measure > 0.45 (not .45) > Numbers with four or more digits
rules.rule_text:
:selected: · For clarity and simplicity, the OECD has adopted the rule that, for all texts in all languages, numbers containing four or more digits are broken by spaces, not punctuation marks.

See also: Punctuation.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 9 Numbers and units of measure > 0.45 (not .45) > Numbers with four or more digits > Do
rules.rule_text: Always use a hard space to separate numbers of four or more digits; never use punctuation nor :selected: run numbers together (4 000, 1 275 103, 8 619 673 021).

rules.section_title: Préambule > 9 Numbers and units of measure > 0.45 (not .45) > Numbers with four or more digits > Don't
rules.rule_text: Don't: :selected: x Break numbers across lines. Use hard spaces to indicate the thousands space. No space is needed if referring to a year, page number, legislation, an address or for online content (2025, p. 1001).

rules.section_title: Préambule > 9 Numbers and units of measure > 0.45 (not .45) > Units of measure
rules.rule_text:
:selected:

. Although most countries and economies use the International System of Units (SI), some continue to use local systems. Use units of measure most appropriate for the topic being discussed.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 9 Numbers and units of measure > 0.45 (not .45) > Units of measure > Do
rules.rule_text:
Separate a number from a unit of measure with a hard space. :selected:

/ Always capitalise units of measure that are derived from a proper name (A [Ampère], Pa [Pascal], :selected: kWh [Watt]).

See also: Breaks and hard spaces.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 10 The OECD and other international organisations
rules.rule_text: International organisations, including the OECD, have particular identities, rules for acronyms and spelling, and ways of presenting themselves. Using correct names, acronyms and titles ensures clarity and avoids offense.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 10 The OECD and other international organisations > Referring to the OECD
rules.rule_text:
. The OECD's full name is the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. Note the British spelling of "organisation" and the hyphen in "co-operation". The acronym is OECD.

· The Organisation's history, membership, wider engagement, ways of working, Secretariat and more are presented on the OECD website: https://www.oecd.org/en/about.html.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 10 The OECD and other international organisations > Referring to the OECD > Do
rules.rule_text:
/ Give the full name followed by the acronym in parentheses on first usage and the acronym or "the Organisation" thereafter.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) is based in Paris, France. The OECD had 38 Member countries as of January 2025. The Organisation is considering the accession of several other countries.

/ Adopt language and key facts from https://www.oecd.org/about when presenting the Organisation orally or in writing.

V Refer to a country with whom Council has opened accession discussions as an "accession :selected: candidate country".

The OECD has 38 Members and 8 accession candidate countries. The Organisation works with more than 100 partner countries and economies around the world, including 5 Key Partners.

:selected: / Capitalise "Associate", "Participant" and "Invitee" if the terms are being used in the context of non-Member participation in the work of in OECD subsidiary bodies in line with the general principals set out in Revised Resolution of the Council on Partnerships in OECD Bodies [C(2012)100/REV2/FINAL].

rules.section_title: Préambule > 11 Punctuation
rules.rule_text: Punctuation marks clarify meaning and indicate pauses, stops or shifts in tone. They help to separate ideas, signal emphasis and convey relationships between parts of a text.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 11 Punctuation > General rules
rules.rule_text:
· Be consistent in the punctuation used throughout the text.

· Use punctuation thoughtfully, without excessive repetition of marks that may confuse the reader.

· Match punctuation to tone and style; some marks may be more appropriate in informal writing than formal.

· In English, never put a space before a colon, comma, exclamation point, full stop (period), question mark or semi-colon.

See also: Capitalisation.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 11 Punctuation > Are Oxford commas necessary? No ... and yes.
rules.rule_text:
The Oxford comma, or serial comma, is used before a conjunction (such as "and", "or") in a list of three or more items. It is more commonly used in American English. OECD usage broadly aligns with British English usage; avoid using the Oxford comma unless necessary for clarity.

· Do not use a comma before the final item in a list. She had soup, bread and salad for lunch.

· Do put a comma before the final item in a list if its omission would cause confusion. They had soup, bread and cheese, and salad for lunch.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 11 Punctuation > Ampersand
rules.rule_text:
· Represented by "&".

· The ampersand represents the word "and".

. It is commonly used in company names and abbreviations as well as in informal writing.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 11 Punctuation > Ampersand > Do
rules.rule_text: V Use the ampersand when part of an official name or title and when commonly used in an abbreviation (Johnson & Johnson, R&D).

rules.section_title: Préambule > 11 Punctuation > Ampersand > Don't
rules.rule_text:
Don't: x Replace "and" with the ampersand in regular text or formal writing.

:selected: The report covers trends in health & education.

The report covers trends in health and education.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 11 Punctuation > Apostrophe
rules.rule_text:
· Represented by """.

· Apostrophes are used with "s" to indicate possession.

· In informal English, apostrophes can be used to indicate contraction.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 11 Punctuation > Apostrophe > Do
rules.rule_text:
:selected: / Place an apostrophe followed by "s" to indicate possession for singular nouns, plural nouns that do not end in "s" and proper names (including those ending in "s").

They considered the prime minister's suggestion. The children's next school holiday is in April. The airline lost Jane's suitcase but not James's suitcase.

/ Place an apostrophe after the "s" for plural nouns that end in "s". :selected: The ministers' decision was unanimous.

V Place the apostrophe after the last name or item in a series. :selected: They met in Jean and Emilia's office to review report.
keywords: for plural nouns that end in

rules.section_title: Préambule > 11 Punctuation > Apostrophe > Don't
rules.rule_text:
Don't: x Use an apostrophe to contract words ("can't" instead of "cannot", "don't" for "do not" or "they're" for "they are") except for informal text where character counts are limited, such as social media. :selected:

x Confuse "its" (a possessive pronoun) and "it's" (a contraction of "it is") or "your" (a possessive :selected: pronoun) and "you're" (a contraction of "you are").

x Use an apostrophe and "s" in decades or abbreviations. :selected: The OECD and several other IO's were founded in the 1960's.

The OECD and several other IOs were founded in the 1960s.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 11 Punctuation > Breaks and hard spaces
rules.rule_text: · Hard spaces between words ensure that words are not split during the document formatting stage.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 11 Punctuation > Breaks and hard spaces > Do
rules.rule_text:
Create hard spaces in Word™ by holding Ctrl + Shift and pressing the space bar. :selected:

V Place a hard space (#) in the cases listed below. :selected:

rules.section_title: Préambule > 11 Punctuation > Required use of hard spaces
rules.rule_text:
Example

Between a person's title and their name

Mr#Smith, Dr#Jones

Between a numeral and the unit or other word accompanying it

page#10, 37#firms, 19th#century

Within numerals made up of four or more digits

20#000#students

Between the day and month (but not month and year) in a date

15#January 2003

In country names

United#States

In currencies

EUR#50, USD#10#million

In units of measure (except ℃ and %)

580#kg, 215#cm, 42#hL

Other examples (depending on context, such as initials or abbreviations)

E.B.#White Smith,#J. (2025) French government e.g.#[text],#etc., et#al.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 11 Punctuation > Colon
rules.rule_text:
· Represented by ":".

· Colons can be used to introduce information or clarification, or for emphasis.

· Use colons sparely: overuse reduces readability.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 11 Punctuation > Colon > Do
rules.rule_text:
:selected: / Use colons to lead into a list, explanation or elaboration or an indented quotation. In most such cases, the colon is preceded by an independent clause.

The OECD is located on two sites: one in Paris and one in Boulogne.

/ Use colons to separate titles and subtitles. :selected: Global Trends in Government Innovation 2024: Fostering Human-Centred Public Services

See also: Capitalisation; Lists.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 11 Punctuation > Colon > Don't
rules.rule_text:
Don't: X Use more than one colon in a sentence. :selected:

x Put a space before a colon. :selected:

x Capitalise the first word after a colon (except for titles). :selected:

rules.section_title: Préambule > 11 Punctuation > Comma
rules.rule_text:
· Represented by ",".

· A comma indicates a brief pause in a sentence. It may also be used to set off specific clauses, phrases or appositives as well as to separate items in a list.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 11 Punctuation > Comma > Do
rules.rule_text:
/ Use commas to separate items in a list.

The Secretary-General visited Japan, Australia and New Zealand.

/ Use a comma to set off a relative clause or other element that is not part of the main sentence. Mr Smith, the committee chair, recommended a fully independent enquiry.

/ Use a comma before conjunction introducing an independent clause. It is one thing to know a gene's chemical structure, but quite another to understand its actual function.

/ Place a comma between adjectives if each modifies the noun alone and if you could insert the word "and" instead of the comma.

The board of directors called for swift, extensive changes.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 11 Punctuation > Comma > Don't
rules.rule_text:
Don't: x Use commas: :selected:

o after "i.e." or "e.g." :unselected:

o before parentheses :unselected:

o before or after en-dashes :unselected:

o before "and" or "or" at the end of a sequence of items, unless one of the items includes another :unselected: "and" or "or".

rules.section_title: Préambule > 11 Punctuation > Ellipses
rules.rule_text:
· Represented by three dots " ... ".

· In formal writing, an ellipsis (plural: ellipses) are used to show that text has been omitted or left unsaid.

· When placed in the middle of a sentence, an ellipsis suggests that something has been taken out; when placed at the end of the sentence, an ellipsis suggests there is more that could be said.

See also: Quotations.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 11 Punctuation > Ellipses > Do
rules.rule_text:
/ Use to indicate material omitted from a quote, with a hard space placed before and after the ellipses (# ... #).

This includes broader sectoral policies to induce emissions reductions by all actors along the supply chain ... as well as policies that induce lifestyle or consumption changes in end users.

/ Place brackets around the ellipsis when a full line or paragraph has been omitted, with a hard space placed before and after (#[ ... ]#).

Governments are using open data initiatives, which foster transparency, accountability and citizen engagement, to improve public services. [ ... ] Open data allows for a collaborative approach to problem-solving.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 11 Punctuation > Ellipses > Don't
rules.rule_text:
Don't: x Break an idea across section headings with ellipses; this is confusing for readers. :selected:

x Use an ellipsis to indicate a pause or to replace "etc." or "and so on". :selected:

x Put parentheses "( )" around an ellipsis. :selected:

x Put spaces between the dots in an ellipsis. :selected:

rules.section_title: Préambule > 11 Punctuation > En-dash
rules.rule_text:
· Represented by "-".

· En-dashes are used to set off information or add a phrase or clause to the sentence.

· En-dashes can be confused with em-dashes and hyphens. See the table "Distinguishing between hyphens and dashes".

rules.section_title: Préambule > 11 Punctuation > En-dash > Do
rules.rule_text:
/ Use an en-dashes in pairs to set off information that is not part of the main sentence, but which you wish to highlight or stress. :selected:

/ Use a space before and after each en-dash. :selected: The conference - for which more than 1 000 participants had registered - lasted three days.

/ Use one en-dash to add a phrase explaining or elaborating on what has gone before. :selected: The meeting was running late - their discussion had been absorbing.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 11 Punctuation > En-dash > Don't
rules.rule_text:
Don't: X Use dashes - of any kind - in titles. :selected:

X Combine dashes with other punctuation; an interjected phrase that starts with a dash must end with one. :selected:

- In a rush - it was late, he dashed out the door.

@ In a rush - it was late - he dashed out the door.

:selected: Use em-dashes

rules.section_title: Préambule > 2013 + ALT x > Forward slash
rules.rule_text:
. They are used to indicate time periods and in expressing ratios and measurements.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 2013 + ALT x > Full stop (period)
rules.rule_text:
· Represented by ".".

· The full stop, or period, indicates the end of a sentence or statement.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 2013 + ALT x > Full stop (period) > Do
rules.rule_text:
/ Use a full stop to complete a sentence and follow it by a space. :selected:

Place a full stop at end of all paragraphs. :selected:

Put the full stop inside quotation marks when it ends the quotation as well as the sentence in which :selected: it appears. Place the full stop outside quotation marks where the quotation itself does not end with a full stop.

The chairperson said, "This meeting is concluded." The report often referred to "ups and downs".

/ Place a full stop after abbreviations such "etc." and where generally customary ("i.e." or "e.g."). :selected:

/ Include full stops when needed to avoid confusion. :selected: No, they do not live at No. 20, their house is at No. 25.

See also: Breaks and hard spaces.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 2013 + ALT x > Full stop (period) > Don't
rules.rule_text:
Don't: x Use a full stop after headings, titles, or bulleted items unless they form a complete sentence. :selected:

x Use a full stop if an abbreviation consists of the first and last letters of a word: Mr, Ms, Ltd, Dr. :selected:

See also: Abbreviations, acronyms and signs.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 2013 + ALT x > Lists
rules.rule_text:
· Lists can be useful to highlight important points or enumerate items.

· Bulleted lists are set off from the text, with a bullet point for each item.

· Numbered lists are run into the text and can use Arabic numbers (1, 2, 3), Roman numerals (i, ii, iii) or lowercase letters (a, b, c) as long as the choice is applied consistently.

· See table "Types of lists".

rules.section_title: Préambule > 2013 + ALT x > Lists > Do
rules.rule_text:
/ Use lists sparingly, to avoid interrupting the flow of your text. :selected:

Apply the same grammatical structure to each item in the list. :selected:

V For lists with complete sentences, use a capital letter to start the first word, and a full stop. :selected:

V For list with incomplete sentences, use a lowercase letter to start the first word and no punctuation. :selected:

/ Use bullet points, numbers (Arabic numbers or Roman numerals) or lowercase letters in roman :selected: type, to mark the items in the list.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 2013 + ALT x > 3. Girls and boys perform better in reading when they read for pleasure in their free time. > Parentheses
rules.rule_text:
· Represented by "( )".

· Parentheses set off material that is not a part of the main sentence, such as an explanation. They are also used for in-text citation of a source.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 2013 + ALT x > 3. Girls and boys perform better in reading when they read for pleasure in their free time. > Parentheses > Do
rules.rule_text:
:selected: Use sparingly to avoid jarring the reader; often commas can replace parentheses.

O Mr Blair (the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom) addressed the United Nations.

@ Mr Blair, the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, addressed the United Nations.

/ Put the full stop before the closing parentheses mark if the phrase in parentheses is a complete sentence.

(The OECD Council met last week.)

/ Put the full stop after the closing parentheses mark if the phrase in parentheses is not a complete sentence.

The committee met to discuss several topics (the latest report, new data and a project proposal).

rules.section_title: Préambule > 2013 + ALT x > 3. Girls and boys perform better in reading when they read for pleasure in their free time. > Question mark
rules.rule_text:
· Represented by "?".

· Question marks are used to indicate direct questions.

See also: Quotations.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 2013 + ALT x > 3. Girls and boys perform better in reading when they read for pleasure in their free time. > Question mark > Do
rules.rule_text:
/ Use to mark direct questions, replacing the full stop. :selected:

/ Use a capital letter to start the first word after the question mark.

Did the reporter read the policy paper? Apparently not.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 2013 + ALT x > 3. Girls and boys perform better in reading when they read for pleasure in their free time. > Question mark > Don't
rules.rule_text:
Don't: X Use a question mark for indirect questions. :selected: The reporter was asked whether she had read the report?

The reporter was asked whether she had read the report.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 2013 + ALT x > 3. Girls and boys perform better in reading when they read for pleasure in their free time. > Quotation marks
rules.rule_text:
· Quotation marks come in pairs: one mark to open the quote and another to close it.

· Single quotation marks are indicated with (''), while double quotation marks are indicated with (" "). Each are used in different ways.

· Quotation marks enclose direct speech, quotations, titles or terms.

See also: Full stop (period); Quotations.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 2013 + ALT x > 3. Girls and boys perform better in reading when they read for pleasure in their free time. > Quotation marks > Do
rules.rule_text:
/ Use double quotation marks for direct speech, short quotations, titles or terms. "The report discusses financial markets in Central and Eastern Europe."

/ Use single quotation marks for quotes within quotes

"The report discusses 'grey markets' in Central and Eastern Europe."

/ Place punctuation after the quotation mark when the quoted material does not end a sentence. The report discusses "grey markets", which are of particular concern in emerging economies.

/ Place punctuation within the quotation mark if the quoted material ends with a full stop. The report concluded that "continued growth is uncertain. The outlook remains cloudy."

/ Put punctuation after the close quotation mark if the quoted material itself does not end with a full stop and ends the sentence.

The speaker asserted that monetary policy must remain "vigilant".

rules.section_title: Préambule > 2013 + ALT x > 3. Girls and boys perform better in reading when they read for pleasure in their free time. > Quotation marks > Don't
rules.rule_text:
Don't: x Use any quotation marks to set off quotations longer than five lines.

x Use single quotation marks for stand-alone terms.

This report refers to all 'participants' as defined below.

This report refers to all "participants" as defined below.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 2013 + ALT x > 3. Girls and boys perform better in reading when they read for pleasure in their free time. > Semi-colon
rules.rule_text:
· Represented by ";".

· Semi-colons connect clauses that could stand alone as separate sentences, but which are linked for emphasis or because they are related.

· Semi-colons also clarify complex lists.

See also: Colon; Lists.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 2013 + ALT x > 3. Girls and boys perform better in reading when they read for pleasure in their free time. > Semi-colon > Do
rules.rule_text:
/ Use semi-colons to join related clauses. :selected:

Separate items in complex lists that contain commas. :selected:

The committee reviewed the report; approval was unanimously given. They visited Paris, France; Rome, Italy; and Athens, Greece.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 2013 + ALT x > 3. Girls and boys perform better in reading when they read for pleasure in their free time. > Semi-colon > Don't
rules.rule_text:
Don't: X Use semi-colons in simple lists. :selected: They invested in Apple; IBM; Dell; and Microsoft. They invested in Apple, IBM, Dell and Microsoft.

x Use semi-colons and colons interchangeably. :selected: The team has one goal; success.

The team has one goal: success.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 2013 + ALT x > 3. Girls and boys perform better in reading when they read for pleasure in their free time. > Square brackets
rules.rule_text:
· Represented by "[ ]".

· The note symbol is placed within square brackets and in subscript (OCDE, 2025[1]).

See also: Quotations.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 2013 + ALT x > 3. Girls and boys perform better in reading when they read for pleasure in their free time. > Square brackets > Do
rules.rule_text:
:selected: / Use square brackets are used within other forms of punctuation, usually parentheses, to provide additional information or explanation.

(We also administered the Beck Depression Inventory [BDI; Beck, Steer, & Garbin, 1988], but those results are not reported here.)

Use within direct quotes to note information not in the original. :selected: The chair said, "At this point [2022], the outlook is still unclear."

rules.section_title: Préambule > 12 Quotations
rules.rule_text: It is essential to correctly format your quotations and cite their sources. Doing so ensures that you respect copyright and avoid plagiarism. It also helps other readers to identify and access your source materials.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 12 Quotations > General rules
rules.rule_text:
· A quotation is a passage taken from another work and clearly indicated as such. A quotation can also present the words and thoughts of third parties reported in the text.

. In order to avoid plagiarism, always fully cite your sources. Further information on plagiarism is available at https://com-apps.oecd.org/com-guidance-portal/en/how-to/how-to-avoid- plagiarism.

See also: Bibliographical references, citations and notes; Punctuation.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 12 Quotations > Long quotes
rules.rule_text:
· Use a separate, indented paragraph for quotes of more than five lines.

· Use the correct O.N.E Author style for long quotes and do not add quotation marks.

· Insert the author name in the "Reference Management" tool in Word™. The reference number will be automatically generated when the reference is added to your bibliography.

. Cite the source in parentheses at the end of the quote and do not put a full stop after the citation.

The global economy has remained resilient this year, despite differences in the strength of activity across countries and sectors. Inflation has continued to moderate and headline inflation is now back to central bank targets in most economies. Labour market tightness has also eased, although unemployment rates generally remain at or near historical lows. However, risks are casting a shadow over what is otherwise a relatively benign central projection. Key risks pertain to the intensification of geopolitical tensions, inflation turning out more persistent than anticipated and a sharp repricing of risk in financial markets. (OECD, 2024[1])

rules.section_title: Préambule > 12 Quotations > Short quotes
rules.rule_text:
· Insert quotes of five lines or less into the running text, using double quotation marks (" ") and in-text citation.

"The global economy has proved resilient. Inflation has declined further towards central bank targets, while growth has remained stable," OECD Secretary-General Mathias Cormann said (OECD, 2024).

rules.section_title: Préambule > 12 Quotations > Quotations and punctuation
rules.rule_text:
· Place punctuation inside the quotation marks if the quote ends the clause or sentence; place outside the quotation marks if not.

"Inflation in the OECD is expected to ease further, from 5.4% in 2024 to 3.8% in 2025 and 3.0% in 2026." (OECD, 2024)

"Inflation in the OECD is expected to ease further" in 2025 and 2026 (OECD, 2024).

· Use single quotation marks ('') for quotes of more than one word within quotes.

"In Figure 2.15, 'green technology' refers to a firm that in the previous two years has invested in products or technologies that reduce its energy consumption or improve its environmental footprint."

· Replace omitted words or phrases with an ellipsis ( ... ); replace omitted paragraphs with an ellipsis in square brackets ([ ... ]).

"A common indicator of labour shortages is the ratio of the number of job vacancies to the number of unemployed individuals. ... By late 2023, vacancies per unemployed had returned to their pre-pandemic trend in the United States, the euro area and Japan." (OECD, 2024)

"In the past few years, the global economy has demonstrated remarkable resilience despite being subject to major shocks. Global trade has also been recovering. [ ... ] Trade has been an important engine of global growth, job creation and declining poverty in the past decades." (OECD, 2024)

· Place square brackets "[ ]" around that has been added to the quotation.

"Trade has been an important engine of growth, job creation and declining poverty in the past decades [in all OECD countries]." (OECD, 2024)

. Use a capital letter to start the quote if the quote is at the start of the sentence or if it follows a colon. Use a lowercase letter if the quote is part of a run on phrase.

"Another source of risk comes from the public finances, as public debt remains at elevated levels," noted the OECD Economic Outlook. (OECD, 2024)

The OECD Economic Outlook argued that "some emerging market economies and low-income countries are now in debt distress". (OECD, 2024)

See also: Ellipses; Square brackets.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 13 Spelling and usage
rules.rule_text: Using correct, consistent spelling in your content conveys your meaning clearly and preserves the Organisation's reputation for accuracy and quality. Selecting the correct terms is also essential.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 13 Spelling and usage > British English spelling
rules.rule_text:
· Use British English spelling in all OECD content.

· The Concise Oxford English Dictionary is the OECD's dictionary of choice.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 13 Spelling and usage > British English spelling > Do
rules.rule_text:
Set your language in Word™ to "English (United Kingdom)".

/ Use "-ise" endings, not "-ize" ("organise", "realise").

/ Use "-our" endings, not "-or" ("labour", "honour").

/ Use "-re" endings, not "er" ("centre", "metre").

y Use double consonants when adding endings to words ("travelling", "focussed", "labelled").

/ Respect the use of American spelling in the names of US institutions or of institutions that use US spelling.

The International Labour Organization is based in Geneva.

rules.section_title: Préambule > 13 Spelling and usage > Choosing the right words
rules.rule_text:
· Use clear, simple language to communicate effectively with audiences who might not be native English speakers or experts in the subject.

· Avoid foreign words and expressions (ceteris paribus, inter alia, ipso facto). They make your writing harder to understand and alternatives exist in English ("other things being equal", "among other things", "by the fact of").

· Be aware that some words in English may be pronounced or spelt similarly yet have very different meanings or may have similar yet not interchangeable meanings. Refer to the table "Commonly confused English words".

. Take care to choose the word that actually expresses your meaning. The table "Commonly misused words in English" helps you to navigate key English words are often that are often used incorrectly.

. Note that some words in English and French share the same meaning but are not spelt exactly the same. The table "Commonly confused spellings of similar words in English and French" highlights key examples of this.

See also: Avoiding confusion between English and French terms.

rules.rule_text:
Explanation

Across (prep.)

Can be ambiguous. "The report presented data on unemployment across several countries" - does this mean data within countries, on each of several countries, or on a group of countries? Be specific. "The report compared the unemployment data of several countries."

Address (verb)

Imprecise. Replace with a more specific word such as "discuss" or "investigate".

All right (adj., adv.)

Always two words. "Alright" is incorrect.

And/or (n/a)

Do not use. Rephrase to "A or B, or both". "You may present your passport or identity card, or both."

Annex (noun)

Always use. Do not use "appendix".

Comprise (verb)

To consist or be made of all the parts of that make up a whole. "The final report comprises six chapters and two annexes." Not a synonym for "contain" or "include". Do not use "is comprised of"; this is incorrect.

Concerted (adj.)

By agreement, in unison. Must be used to refer to one or more countries, institutions or individuals; one alone cannot make a concerted effort.

Consensus (noun)

Means "shared opinion", not "majority view".

Constitute (verb)

The parts that make up a whole. "The House of Commons and the House of Lords constitute the Parliament of the United Kingdom." Not to be confused with "contain": "This report contains the group's findings, the result of three years of work" (correct) but "This report constitutes three years of work" (incorrect).

Impact (noun)

Do not use as a verb: "The policy had a direct impact on pollution" (correct) but "The policy impacted pollution" (incorrect).

Implement (verb)

Means "carry out", "execute", "accomplish". Much overused, employ synonyms when possible.

In regard to (prep.)

"In regard to" is the proper expression; use "regard" (with no "s") rather than "regards".

Include (verb)

Means "part of a whole", does not mean "comprise". "The countries supporting this policy include Denmark, Norway and Sweden." In this example, using "include" means that at least one other country supports the policy. Do not use the phrase "including but not limited to"; it is redundant.

Literally (adv.)

Something happened exactly as described. "They literally drove five hours to attend the event." Only use in this sense. Does not mean "in effect" or "virtually". "He literally exploded" would mean there were bits of him all over the walls, floor and ceiling. Do not use metaphorically.

Loan (noun)

Means "an amount of borrowed money". "The firm has repaid the loan." Do not use as a verb, use "lend". "The bank lends money at a fixed interest rate."

Presently (adv.)

Do not use, to avoid confusion between the difference in its meaning between British English ("soon") and American
English ("now").

Regardless (adv.)

Means "despite" or "not affected by". "Regardless of their department, all staff are encouraged to contribute ideas." Do not use "irregardless"; it is a double negative and is not equivalent to "regardless".

Regime (noun)

Means "government or system of government", "a particular way of doing something". If used refer to the government of a country, usually implies dictatorship and is considered pejorative. Do not use in this context.

Regular (adj.)

Means "at regular intervals". "Halley's comet regularly approaches the Earth, appearing in the skies every 76 years". Does not mean "frequent".

Scheme (noun)

Means "plan" or "project". Do not use as it carries a negative connotation of "sneaky" or "devious" in American English. Use instead a word that is neutral in both British and American English ("programme", "project", "plan" or "initiative").
